what_its_for: Enzalutamide is used to treat prostate cancer. It works by blocking the effects of male hormones (like testosterone) that can help prostate cancer cells grow. It is used in men whose prostate cancer has spread to other parts of the body or continues to grow despite other treatments.
how_to_take: Swallow the capsules or tablets whole with or without food. Do not crush, chew, or open the capsules. Take enzalutamide at the same time every day to help you remember. If you vomit after taking your dose, do not take another dose that day — just take your next scheduled dose as usual.
dosing: The usual dose is 160 mg (four 40 mg capsules or tablets) taken by mouth once daily. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions, as your dose may be adjusted based on side effects or other medications you are taking. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store enzalutamide at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep the medication in its original container with the cap tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medication safely — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires alertness until you know how this medicine affects you, because it can cause dizziness, mental changes, or seizures. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as they may affect how the drug works in your body. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL other medications you take, including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, and herbal supplements, because enzalutamide interacts with many medications. Women who are pregnant or may become pregnant should NOT handle this medication, as it can harm an unborn baby. Men taking this drug should use effective birth control during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose if their partner could become pregnant.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a seizure (shaking, loss of consciousness, confusion); signs of a serious brain condition called PRES such as sudden severe headache, vision changes, confusion, or loss of coordination; severe dizziness or fainting; signs of heart problems such as chest pain or shortness of breath; unusual fractures or falls; memory problems or significant mood changes; numbness or weakness in your arms or legs; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you notice any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Enzalutamide begins working right away at the cellular level, but you may not feel or notice a difference immediately. Your doctor will monitor your response through blood tests (such as PSA levels) and imaging scans over weeks to months. It is important to keep taking your medicine every day even if you feel well, as stopping early can allow the cancer to grow.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Enzalutamide is commonly used in older men. Be extra cautious about fall risk due to dizziness and muscle weakness. Kidney or liver problems: Dose adjustments may be needed for severe liver disease; tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions. Women and children: Enzalutamide is not approved for use in women or children. Pregnant women must avoid handling this medication. Men with seizure history: Use with caution — tell your doctor if you have ever had a seizure, a brain injury, a stroke, or brain tumors, as this medicine can increase the risk of seizures.
